title: The Stanley Hotel: The Real Story Behind The Shining

lines.say: On October 30th, 1974, the night before Halloween, a young writer and his wife checked into an old hotel in the Colorado Rockies.
lines.tts: On October 30th, nineteen seventy-four, the night before Halloween, a young writer and his wife checked into an old hotel in the Colorado Rockies.

lines.say: It was about to close for the winter. As he told it later, they were the only guests in the place.
At dinner, theirs was the only table set. Every other chair was up on the tables, while recorded orchestra music played to the empty room.
lines.lower: Drawn for this film | the story as Stephen King told it

lines.say: That night, he dreamed that his three-year-old son was running down the hotel's hallways, looking back over his shoulder, screaming. He was being chased by a fire hose.
He woke up drenched in sweat, lit a cigarette, and sat looking out the window at the mountains. By the time he'd finished it, he had the bones of a novel.
The writer was Stephen King. The book became The Shining. And the hotel was the Stanley.
But the Stanley's story starts more than seventy years earlier, with a man from Maine who came to these mountains expecting to die.

lines.say: Freelan Oscar Stanley was born on June 1st, 1849, in Kingfield, Maine. He had an identical twin, Francis. People knew them as F.O. and F.E.
lines.tts: Freelan Oscar Stanley was born on June 1st, eighteen forty-nine, in Kingfield, Maine. He had an identical twin, Francis. People knew them as F.O. and F.E.

lines.say: The twins were inventors. Their company made photographic dry plates, and in 1905, they sold it to Eastman Kodak.
lines.tts: The twins were inventors. Their company made photographic dry plates, and in nineteen oh five, they sold it to Eastman Kodak.

lines.say: By then, they had a new business: steam-powered automobiles. The Stanley Steamer.
In 1906, a Stanley steam racer set a world speed record on the sand at Ormond Beach, Florida: more than 127 miles an hour.
lines.tts: In nineteen oh six, a Stanley steam racer set a world speed record on the sand at Ormond Beach, Florida: more than a hundred and twenty-seven miles an hour.

lines.say: But F.O. Stanley was sick. He had survived tuberculosis once, in 1881, the year the disease killed one of his brothers. In 1903, it came back, and this time it looked like it would kill him.
lines.tts: But F.O. Stanley was sick. He had survived tuberculosis once, in eighteen eighty-one, the year the disease killed one of his brothers. In nineteen oh three, it came back, and this time it looked like it would kill him.

lines.say: The treatment of the day was fresh, dry air, sunshine and rest. Stanley went west to Denver, where a tuberculosis doctor sent him higher, to a mountain valley he compared to the famous health resorts of Switzerland: Estes Park.
Stanley arrived on June 30th, 1903, with his wife, Flora.
lines.tts: Stanley arrived on June 30th, nineteen oh three, with his wife, Flora.

lines.say: The mountains worked, or something did. He got better. He would live another thirty-seven years.
Stanley fell in love with the valley. He and Flora built a summer house there, and he decided to build a grand hotel, for friends from back East who came out to visit.
He bought the land from the ranch of an Irish earl, Lord Dunraven, who back in the 1870s had tried to take over the whole valley as his private hunting preserve.
lines.tts: He bought the land from the ranch of an Irish earl, Lord Dunraven, who back in the eighteen seventies had tried to take over the whole valley as his private hunting preserve.

lines.say: Construction began in 1907. Stanley helped design it himself, in the Colonial Revival style of the East: white walls, red roofs and a long porch facing the peaks.
lines.tts: Construction began in nineteen oh seven. Stanley helped design it himself, in the Colonial Revival style of the East: white walls, red roofs and a long porch facing the peaks.

lines.say: To light it, he built a hydroelectric plant on the Fall River, which brought electricity to Estes Park for the first time.
Getting there was half the adventure. Guests rode the train as far as Lyons, in the foothills. From there, Stanley's company carried them up the canyon in steam-powered Mountain Wagons.
The Stanley Hotel opened on July 4th, 1909.
lines.tts: The Stanley Hotel opened on July 4th, nineteen oh nine.

lines.say: That same year, he built a concert hall beside it, for Flora, who played the piano.
He also helped bring elk back to the valley from Yellowstone, in 1913, and backed the campaign for Rocky Mountain National Park, which was created right next door in 1915.
lines.tts: He also helped bring elk back to the valley from Yellowstone, in nineteen thirteen, and backed the campaign for Rocky Mountain National Park, which was created right next door in nineteen fifteen.

lines.say: It was a summer resort, for wealthy travelers, and for people who came west for their health, the way Stanley had. For decades, the hotel had no heat. Every fall, it closed for the winter.
On June 25th, 1911, in the hotel's third summer, a gas explosion went off inside the Stanley.
lines.tts: On June 25th, nineteen eleven, in the hotel's third summer, a gas explosion went off inside the Stanley.

lines.say: As the hotel tells the story, the power was out, and a chambermaid named Elizabeth Wilson walked into Room 217 with a flame, not knowing the room was full of gas.
lines.tts: As the hotel tells the story, the power was out, and a chambermaid named Elizabeth Wilson walked into Room two-seventeen with a flame, not knowing the room was full of gas.

lines.say: The newspapers reported eight workers hurt, and no guests. The worst hurt was the chambermaid. The Associated Press said she was hurled from the second floor to the first, and that both her ankles were broken.

Not every paper agreed. Colorado papers gave her name as Elizabeth Lambert. And four days later, the Fort Collins Express printed a long, detailed account saying she had never fallen through the floor at all.

lines.say: She survived. In the hotel's telling, she healed, went back to work at the Stanley, and stayed for years.
Remember that room number: 217.
lines.tts: Remember that room number: two-seventeen.

lines.say: In 1926, Stanley sold the hotel. The company that bought it went broke, so he took it back, and in 1930, he sold it again.
lines.tts: In nineteen twenty-six, Stanley sold the hotel. The company that bought it went broke, so he took it back, and in nineteen thirty, he sold it again.

lines.say: Flora died in 1939. Freelan Oscar Stanley died the next year, on October 2nd, 1940. He was ninety-one.
lines.tts: Flora died in nineteen thirty-nine. Freelan Oscar Stanley died the next year, on October 2nd, nineteen forty. He was ninety-one.

lines.say: The hotel passed from owner to owner. With no heat, it still shut down every winter. By the 1970s, its glory days seemed long gone, and the hotel's own history admits it might have ended up under the wrecking ball.

lines.say: Then, in 1974, another man from Maine moved to Colorado.
lines.tts: Then, in nineteen seventy-four, another man from Maine moved to Colorado.

Two years earlier, he'd started a novel called Darkshine, about a psychic boy in a psychic amusement park. He had given up on it.

lines.say: Then came that night at the Stanley. The empty halls. The music playing to no one. The dream.
The hotel says the Kings stayed in Room 217.

lines.say: In the book, a struggling writer named Jack Torrance takes a job as the winter caretaker of the Overlook, a mountain resort that's snowed in for months. He brings his wife, Wendy, and their son, Danny, who has a gift: the shining.

lines.say: The hotel's ghosts go to work on Jack. And the one room Danny is warned to stay out of is Room 217.

lines.say: The Shining came out in January 1977. It was King's third novel, and his first hardcover bestseller.
lines.tts: The Shining came out in January nineteen seventy-seven. It was King's third novel, and his first hardcover bestseller.

lines.say: That May, the Stanley Hotel was added to the National Register of Historic Places.
In 1980, Stanley Kubrick turned the book into a movie, with Jack Nicholson as Jack Torrance.
lines.tts: In nineteen eighty, Stanley Kubrick turned the book into a movie, with Jack Nicholson as Jack Torrance.

lines.say: Kubrick didn't film at the Stanley. The outside of his Overlook is Timberline Lodge, on Mount Hood in Oregon, and the inside was built on sound stages in England.
Timberline asked for one change. Its managers were afraid guests would refuse to sleep in the lodge's real Room 217. So in the movie, it's Room 237, a number Timberline doesn't have.
lines.tts: Timberline asked for one change. Its managers were afraid guests would refuse to sleep in the lodge's real Room two-seventeen. So in the movie, it's Room two-thirty-seven, a number Timberline doesn't have.

lines.say: King never liked Kubrick's version. In 1997, he made his own, a TV miniseries, and this time it was filmed at the Stanley.
lines.tts: King never liked Kubrick's version. In nineteen ninety-seven, he made his own, a TV miniseries, and this time it was filmed at the Stanley.

lines.say: Hollywood kept coming back. In Dumb and Dumber, the Stanley played a fancy hotel in Aspen.
And in 2015, the hotel planted a hedge maze, a nod to Kubrick's film. There's no hedge maze in King's book. He wrote topiary animals instead, the kind that move when you aren't looking.

lines.say: Ever since The Shining, people have come to the Stanley hoping to meet a ghost. Some say they have.
In Room 217, guests tell of a presence that tidies up: suitcases unpacked, clothes folded and put away, lights switched off. They say it's the chambermaid from 1911.
lines.tts: In Room two-seventeen, guests tell of a presence that tidies up: suitcases unpacked, clothes folded and put away, lights switched off. They say it's the chambermaid from nineteen eleven.

lines.say: Some say she doesn't approve of unmarried couples sharing a bed.
On the fourth floor, guests report hearing children laughing and running in the halls at night. When they look, no one's there. And there's no known record of a child ever dying there.
Some say they've seen F.O. Stanley himself, in the billiard room and the bar. And in the music room, people say Flora's piano sometimes plays by itself.
Ghost-hunting TV shows have investigated the hotel, and it runs ghost tours of its own.
None of it has ever been proven. And according to the Denver Gazette, an employee caught faking a haunting can be fired.
Since 1983, the Stanley has stayed open all year. In 2025, it was sold in a four-hundred-million-dollar deal, to a nonprofit created through a Colorado state authority.
lines.tts: Since nineteen eighty-three, the Stanley has stayed open all year. In twenty twenty-five, it was sold in a four-hundred-million-dollar deal, to a nonprofit created through a Colorado state authority.

lines.say: On the grounds, construction is under way on the Stanley Film Center, with a new theater and a museum of horror films. It's set to open in 2028.
lines.tts: On the grounds, construction is under way on the Stanley Film Center, with a new theater and a museum of horror films. It's set to open in twenty twenty-eight.

lines.say: F.O. Stanley came west expecting to die, and lived thirty-seven more years. The hotel he built nearly faded away, until a writer spent one night there, and had a nightmare.
Is the Stanley haunted? You'll have to decide that for yourself. But few buildings owe as much to a ghost story.
